method: A knife pleat folds once, so one pleat eats twice its depth and shows one depth of fabric; a box pleat and an inverted pleat fold twice, so one pleat eats four times its depth and shows two. The flat space between pleats is counted once per pleat. The fabric a pleat takes is the spacing plus twice the depth for a knife pleat and the spacing plus four times the depth for a box or inverted pleat, so twelve knife pleats one inch deep with two inches between them take four inches each, forty eight inches in total. The pleated width is the pleat count times what each pleat shows, which is three inches each in the same example, thirty six inches. The folded-away figure is the difference between the two and is the fabric that disappears into the folds. The fullness ratio is the fabric divided by the pleated width, so a ratio of two to one means the panel is cut twice its finished width. Strips are counted by dividing the fabric by the usable fabric width and rounding up, so the forty eight inch pleat run on forty four inch fabric is two strips of twenty four inches; an exact fit stays one strip. Inches and centimetres are both supported; the arithmetic is unit-free and the page also shows the fabric converted at exactly 2.54 centimetres to the inch. Inputs are limited to 1 to 200 whole pleats, a depth of 0.1 to 24 inches (0.25 to 60 centimetres), a spacing of 0 to 24 inches (0 to 60 centimetres) and a usable width of 1 to 120 inches (2.5 to 305 centimetres); text, negative numbers, exponent notation, empty fields and out of range values are refused with the field named. The page assumes the pleats run across one flat panel with even spacing and equal depth, and does not model pattern repeat, nap or directional print, seam allowances, a heading or waistband, pleats that taper or meet at a seam, or the pressing and stitching order; it stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

sources.title: Sewing and pattern-drafting practice: a knife pleat uses twice its depth of fabric and shows one depth, while a box or inverted pleat uses four times its depth because it folds to both sides.
Dressmaking fullness guidance: a pleated panel is cut roughly one and a half to three times its finished width, depending on the pleat depth and the space left between pleats.
Sewing construction practice: pleats are marked and pressed before stitching, and a pleat run wider than the fabric is cut in strips joined at a seam.
